Solution II: dynamical approach

When the cylinder is displaced from its equilibrium position
downwards by distance x1 , the net restoring force (pointing up)
can be calculated as the sum of the weight of the cylinder and
the force from the difference of pressures at the top (p0 ) and bot-
tom (p) of the cylinder. As a result of the net force, the cylinder

accelerates upwards with a1 , and at the same time, the liquid lo-
cated in the gap between the cylinder and the wall of the beaker

accelerates down with a2 . The relation between the magnitudes

of a1 and a2 is given by the continuity law:

                        sa1 = (S − s)a2 .

                                Fig. 2

If the liquid in the gap was not accelerating, the pressure differ-
ence p − p0 would be equal to the hydrostatic pressure of the
liquid column in the gap. Due to the acceleration of the liquid,
p − p0 can be expressed from Newton’s 2nd law applied for the

liquid column of unit area located in the gap:

       p0 − p + ϱg(γh + x1 + x2 ) = ϱ(γh + x1 + x2 )a2 ,

where we used the notations of Solution I, and the downward
direction was taken as positive.

  Newton’s 2nd law for the cylinder reads as

                 (p − p0 )s − γϱshg = γϱsha1 .

After expressing p − p0 from the previous equation, and then
substituting it here we get:

ϱg(γh+x1 +x2 )s−ϱ(γh+x1 +x2 )a2 s−γϱshg = γϱsha1 .

Since the amplitude of the liquid level is small, the terms con-

taining a2 x1 and a2 x2 can be neglected. After rearranging we

get:

               ϱgs(x1 + x2 ) = γϱsh(a1 + a2 ) .

Using the relations between the displacements and accelera-
tions we finally get:
